bridges.name: Cherry Avenue Bridge
bridges.fact: A rare bobtail swing bridge that pivots on the bank. It carries a rail spur, cyclists and pedestrians onto Goose Island. A Chicago Landmark.

bridges.name: Halsted Street Bridge (canal)
bridges.fact: A steel tied arch that replaced a 1908 bascule bridge. The canal it crosses was dug in the 1850s and turned this land into Goose Island.

bridges.name: Outer Drive Bridge (DuSable Lake Shore Drive)
bridges.fact: When it opened in 1937 it was the longest and widest bascule bridge in the world. President Franklin Roosevelt dedicated it.

bridges.name: Columbus Drive Bridge
bridges.fact: One of the largest bascule bridges anywhere, with steel box girders instead of trusses.

bridges.name: DuSable Bridge (Michigan Avenue)
bridges.fact: The first double-deck bascule bridge with roadways on both levels. Its four bridgehouses carry sculptures of scenes from Chicago history; one houses the bridgehouse museum.

bridges.name: Dearborn Street Bridge
bridges.fact: Chicago's first movable bridge, a rope-drawn drawbridge, was built at this crossing in 1834.

bridges.name: La Salle Street Bridge (Marshall Suloway Bridge)
Kinzie Street Railroad Bridge
bridges.fact: The Chicago & North Western bridge, the longest and heaviest bascule leaf in the world when built. The last train crossed in 2000 and it has stood locked upright since. A Chicago Landmark.

bridges.name: Kinzie Street Bridge
bridges.fact: In 1992 pilings driven into the riverbed beside this bridge broke into an old freight tunnel and flooded basements across the Loop.

bridges.name: Ohio Street Bridge
bridges.fact: Carries the feeder ramps of the Kennedy Expressway.

bridges.name: Chicago Avenue Bridge
bridges.fact: The 1914 bascule bridge was removed in 2018. A fixed bridge carries the street while a permanent replacement is planned.

bridges.name: Division Street Bridge (river)
bridges.fact: The west crossing of Goose Island, among the oldest bascule bridges left in the city.

bridges.name: Lake Street Bridge
bridges.fact: The first double-deck bascule bridge in the city: the street below, Green and Pink Line trains above.

bridges.name: Ida B. Wells Drive Bridge
bridges.fact: Two parallel bridges carrying the road that becomes the Eisenhower Expressway.

bridges.name: Roosevelt Road Bridge
bridges.fact: Built when this stretch of the river was straightened, between 1928 and 1930, to make room for rail yards and streets.

bridges.name: St. Charles Air Line Bridge
bridges.fact: When finished it was the longest single-leaf bascule in the world. It was shortened and moved here when the river was straightened. Beside it stands the Baltimore & Ohio bridge, locked upright.

bridges.name: Canal Street Railroad Bridge
bridges.fact: The only vertical-lift bridge on the river. Amtrak and Metra trains cross between towers 195 feet high. A Chicago Landmark.

bridges.name: Cermak Road Bridge
bridges.fact: The last Scherzer rolling-lift bridge still working on the river: the leaves rock back on curved girders like a rocking chair.

pois.name: Lake Michigan
pois.f: The tour starts on the open lake, outside the breakwaters that shelter Chicago Harbor.

pois.name: Navy Pier
pois.f: Opened in 1916 as Municipal Pier, 3,300 feet long. It has been a freight and passenger dock, a Navy training base in both world wars and a university campus. The Centennial Wheel stands near its landward end.

pois.name: Chicago Harbor Lock
pois.f: Finished in 1938. The river was reversed in 1900 to flow away from the lake, and the lock keeps lake water from pouring into it. It is one of the busiest locks in the country.

pois.name: Centennial Fountain
pois.f: In summer it shoots an arc of water across the river once an hour. It marks the centennial of the agency that reversed the river.

pois.name: Chicago Riverwalk
pois.f: A pedestrian path along the south bank of the Main Stem, running from the lake to Lake Street.

pois.name: Wolf Point
pois.f: The fork where the Main Stem meets the North and South branches. The city's first taverns and hotel stood here in the 1820s and 30s. The Y of the three branches is the symbol on Chicago's municipal device.

pois.name: Goose Island
pois.f: An artificial island, created in the 1850s when the North Branch Canal was dug along its east side. Long an industrial district, now also offices and breweries.

pois.name: North Avenue Turning Basin
pois.f: The wide water at the north tip of Goose Island, where ships could turn around. The tour turns back here and comes down the canal.

pois.name: Ping Tom Memorial Park
pois.f: Chinatown's riverfront park, on a former rail yard. The water taxi from downtown lands here. End of the tour.
